title: FLOWBUDGET: TRAINING-FREE SAMPLING-BUDGET ESTIMATION FOR FLOW MATCHING MODELS

paper.title: FLOWBUDGET: TRAINING-FREE SAMPLING-BUDGET ESTIMATION FOR FLOW MATCHING MODELS
paper.abstract: Abstract Sampling from continuous flow-based generators such as flow matching models requires numerical ODE or SDE integration, making inference cost depend on the number of function evaluations (NFEs). In practice, the sampling budget is inherited from prior work or selected through expensive FID-versus-NFE sweeps, using FID to assess image-generation quality, requiring sample generation and evaluation at multiple budgets. This makes sampling-budget selection dependent on repeated empirical evaluation. We therefore ask a complementary question to solver design and timestep allocation: for a fixed pretrained model and solver, what numerical resolution is sufficient? We introduce FlowBudget , a training-free estimator of solver-relative sampling complexity. Using simulation-free interpolation probes of the learned dynamics, FlowBudget normalizes the leading one-step discretization error by the motion, estimates its coefficient from interpolation probes, and maps a numerical tolerance to a step budget using the solver order. We derive estimators for numerical solvers in flow matching sampling, namely Euler and Heun for ODE sampling and additive-noise Euler–Maruyama for SDE sampling, and connect the ODE coefficients to terminal integration error. Experiments on SiT, FlowDCN and Rectified Flow models, spanning flow-model architectures and formulations, test whether FlowBudget can estimate the NFE budget without generating samples at multiple budgets or performing an FID-versus-NFE sweep. The code is available at https://github.com/Yasaman-dt/FlowBudget .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Flow matching models learn a time-dependent velocity field whose integration transports a reference law to data [ 14 , 15 , 1 ] , and are used across image [ 6 ] , audio [ 12 , 21 ] , and video [ 10 ] generation. At inference, generation requires numerical integration of ordinary differential equations (ODEs) or stochastic differential equations (SDEs) parameterized by the learned model [ 4 , 2 , 20 , 17 ] . Because each integration step requires one or more neural-network evaluations, the solver and its number of function evaluations (NFEs) directly determine sampling cost. Few NFEs can produce substantial discretization error, whereas increasing NFEs reduces this error according to the convergence order of the chosen solver [ 8 , 16 , 19 ] . In practice, however, the number of NFEs is often inherited from a reference implementation, e.g., 250 NFEs [ 17 , 22 ] , or selected by trial and error based on generation quality. Generation error can arise from both approximation error in the learned velocity field and numerical error introduced by the solver. For a fixed pretrained model, the former is fixed, so we focus on the numerical integration error. Recent methods improve sampling efficiency by changing the solver or by allocating a fixed budget nonuniformly [ 16 , 19 , 18 , 7 , 13 , 3 ] . In particular, SharpEuler uses trajectory acceleration—the leading Euler local-error quantity—to decide where a prescribed Euler budget should be spent [ 7 ] . Our problem is complementary: we keep the pretrained model and solver fixed and ask how large the total budget should be . Thus, the novelty is not the use of local truncation error itself, but its use to define and estimate a solver-relative numerical sampling complexity before performing a quality-versus-NFE sweep. We introduce FlowBudget , which associates each pretrained model–solver pair with a scale-normalized numerical-complexity coefficient. Estimated from simulation-free interpolation probes, this coefficient combines with the solver order to map a prescribed relative numerical tolerance directly to a sampling-step budget. Our contributions are threefold. First, we formulate fixed-solver budget estimation as a numerical-error problem and derive a general scaling law relating a stabilized relative local-error tolerance to the required step budget. Second, we instantiate the construction for Euler and Heun ODE sampling and additive-noise Euler–Maruyama sampling, and connect the Euler/Heun differential coefficients to terminal ODE integration error under standard stability assumptions. We also distinguish the population numerical-complexity coefficient from its Monte Carlo estimate and give a finite-probe concentration guarantee. Third, across pretrained SiT, Rectified Flow, and FlowDCN models, we test whether this numerical resolution yields useful quality–cost operating points without using FID-versus-NFE sweeps to construct the estimator.

We evaluate FlowBudget across six pretrained models: SiT-XL/2 [ 17 ] and FlowDCN-XL/2 [ 22 ] on ImageNet [ 5 ] , and RF-UNet, 1-RF, 2-RF, and 3-RF [ 15 ] on CIFAR-10 [ 11 ] , using the solvers from their original works and additionally with Heun for FlowDCN. sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: FlowBudget estimates a fixed solver’s numerical resolution from scale-normalized local discretization error, without an NFE–quality sweep. The Euler, Heun, and additive-noise Euler–Maruyama laws are numerical statements; for ODE solvers, the normalized coefficients also control terminal integration error under a bounded-velocity assumption. Limitations and Future Work. A limitation is that interpolation probes use training-distribution samples and only approximate the sampler trajectory law. Future work will study calibration between τ \tau and perceptual metrics such as FID.

In practice, the sampling budget is inherited from prior work or selected through expensive FID-versus-NFE sweeps, using FID to assess image-generation quality, requiring sample generation and evaluation at multiple budgets. This makes sampling-budget selection dependent on repeated empirical evaluation. We therefore ask a complementary question to solver design and timestep allocation: for a fixed pretrained model and solver, what numerical resolution is sufficient? We introduce FlowBudget , a training-free estimator of solver-relative sampling complexity. Using simulation-free interpolation probes of the learned dynamics, FlowBudget normalizes the leading one-step discretization error by the motion, estimates its coefficient from interpolation probes, and maps a numerical tolerance to a step budget using the solver order. We derive estimators for numerical solvers in flow matching sampling, namely Euler and Heun for ODE sampling and additive-noise Euler–Maruyama for SDE sampling, and connect the ODE coefficients to terminal integration error. Experiments on SiT, FlowDCN and Rectified Flow models, spanning flow-model architectures and formulations, test whether FlowBudget can estimate the NFE budget without generating samples at multiple budgets or performing an FID-versus-NFE sweep. The code is available at https://github.com/Yasaman-dt/FlowBudget . Index Terms: flow matching, generative models, NFE, numerical sampling complexity, ODE/SDE † † address: 1 ÉTS Montréal, 2 LIVIA, 3 ILLS, 4 Mila – Quebec AI Institute, 5 CNRS, CentraleSupélec – Université Paris-Saclay 1 Introduction Flow matching models learn a time-dependent velocity field whose integration transports a reference law to data [ 14 , 15 , 1 ] , and are used across image [ 6 ] , audio [ 12 , 21 ] , and video [ 10 ] generation. At inference, generation requires numerical integration of ordinary differential equations (ODEs) or stochastic differential equations (SDEs) parameterized by the learned model [ 4 , 2 , 20 , 17 ] . Because each integration step requires one or more neural-network evaluations, the solver and its number of function evaluations (NFEs) directly determine sampling cost. Few NFEs can produce substantial discretization error, whereas increasing NFEs reduces this error according to the convergence order of the chosen solver [ 8 , 16 , 19 ] . In practice, however, the number of NFEs is often inherited from a reference implementation, e.g., 250 NFEs [ 17 , 22 ] , or selected by trial and error based on generation quality. Generation error can arise from both approximation error in the learned velocity field and numerical error introduced by the solver. For a fixed pretrained model, the former is fixed, so we focus on the numerical integration error. Recent methods improve sampling efficiency by changing the solver or by allocating a fixed budget nonuniformly [ 16 , 19 , 18 , 7 , 13 , 3 ] . In particular, SharpEuler uses trajectory acceleration—the leading Euler local-error quantity—to decide where a prescribed Euler budget should be spent [ 7 ] . Our problem is complementary: we keep the pretrained model and solver fixed and ask how large the total budget should be . Thus, the novelty is not the use of local truncation error itself, but its use to define and estimate a solver-relative numerical sampling complexity before performing a quality-versus-NFE sweep. We introduce FlowBudget , which associates each pretrained model–solver pair with a scale-normalized numerical-complexity coefficient. Estimated from simulation-free interpolation probes, this coefficient combines with the solver order to map a prescribed relative numerical tolerance directly to a sampling-step budget. Our contributions are threefold. First, we formulate fixed-solver budget estimation as a numerical-error problem and derive a general scaling law relating a stabilized relative local-error tolerance to the required step budget. Second, we instantiate the construction for Euler and Heun ODE sampling and additive-noise Euler–Maruyama sampling, and connect the Euler/Heun differential coefficients to terminal ODE integration error under standard stability assumptions. We also distinguish the population numerical-complexity coefficient from its Monte Carlo estimate and give a finite-probe concentration guarantee.
